Winter precipitation, primarily in the form of snow, will be possible later today into Saturday. The heaviest snow amounts are still expected in parts of northern OK.

(A marginal risk is only 1 out of 5 in terms of severity, so severe storms certainly won't be widespread.) The primary threat is damaging wind gusts. column9: It's a busy afternoon in Middle Tennessee! Rain just won't stop for areas north of I-40. If you had a good soaking rain last night and nearby creeks and ditches are swollen, then you will be more susceptible to flooding this afternoon and evening as repeated waves of heavy rain move over the area. If you come across a water covered roadway, find an alternate route or wait for the water to subside. We promise water won't stay high forever. Now, for the severe weather threat. It's a little uncertain that we'll see any severe weather, but we have a good chance of seeing some strong winds in some storms, especially south of I-40. A few strong cells north of 40 aren't out of the question, just much less likely. We'll be keeping an eye on storms moving up out of Mississippi and west Tennessee this evening. Our best chance of severe or strong storms will be with those. Rain and storms will taper off from west to east this evening from 6PM to Midnight.

A lot of you will take the morning train because you're working 9 to 5. We'll still be here working for the weekend, and the weather this weekend is London calling (mizzling and chilly). Temperatures will turn colder starting on Tuesday, and then, come Wednesday, here we are with open arms. We'll be walking on sunshine and it's time to feelgood. column9: 11:!5 AM - we wanted to share this slightly technical update with you on the developing severe weather potential. Summary; tornado potential will increase after 1pm in western Oklahoma. Stay alert! The warm front has moved to roughly one county south of Interstate 40. This has allowed surface based instability to increase markedly over southern OK. One of the challenges now is to determine how far north the front will move before stalling this afternoon. Ongoing elevated storms in northern OK have generated a cold pool of outflow air that will eventually serve to limit the front's northern extent. Our present expectation is that the front will continue moving north, then stall when it encounters the cold pool. We expect that position to be about one county north of Interstate 40 by 1-2 pm. Along and south of this boundary the combination of strong shear and strong instability will be sufficient to support supercells with long track, intense tornadoes. We will be monitoring this warm sector from here on out for convective initiation. Confidence is high for severe storms to also develop along the dry line in West TX and threaten western OK and western North Texas late this afternoon and evening. In summary, the shear and instability in the warm sector is unusually favorable for intense tornadoes. This will be a protracted period of threat, lasting into the overnight hours. We are also dedicating extra resources to monitor the developing hydrologic situation. Exceptionally high rainfall rates in will result in significant and potentially life threatening flash flooding. It's important this message not be lost in the overall concern over tornadoes. This factor needs to be considered as sheltering plans are made. Additional updates will follow this afternoon.

column9: 11:!5 AM - we wanted to share this slightly technical update with you on the developing severe weather potential. Summary; tornado potential will increase after 1pm in western Oklahoma. Stay alert! The warm front has moved to roughly one county south of Interstate 40. This has allowed surface based instability to increase markedly over southern OK. One of the challenges now is to determine how far north the front will move before stalling this afternoon. Ongoing elevated storms in northern OK have generated a cold pool of outflow air that will eventually serve to limit the front's northern extent. Our present expectation is that the front will continue moving north, then stall when it encounters the cold pool. We expect that position to be about one county north of Interstate 40 by 1-2 pm. Along and south of this boundary the combination of strong shear and strong instability will be sufficient to support supercells with long track, intense tornadoes. We will be monitoring this warm sector from here on out for convective initiation. Confidence is high for severe storms to also develop along the dry line in West TX and threaten western OK and western North Texas late this afternoon and evening. In summary, the shear and instability in the warm sector is unusually favorable for intense tornadoes. This will be a protracted period of threat, lasting into the overnight hours. We are also dedicating extra resources to monitor the developing hydrologic situation. Exceptionally high rainfall rates in will result in significant and potentially life threatening flash flooding. It's important this message not be lost in the overall concern over tornadoes. This factor needs to be considered as sheltering plans are made. Additional updates will follow this afternoon.

column9: 11:!5 AM - we wanted to share this slightly technical update with you on the developing severe weather potential. Summary; tornado potential will increase after 1pm in western Oklahoma. Stay alert! The warm front has moved to roughly one county south of Interstate 40. This has allowed surface based instability to increase markedly over southern OK. One of the challenges now is to determine how far north the front will move before stalling this afternoon. Ongoing elevated storms in northern OK have generated a cold pool of outflow air that will eventually serve to limit the front's northern extent. Our present expectation is that the front will continue moving north, then stall when it encounters the cold pool. We expect that position to be about one county north of Interstate 40 by 1-2 pm. Along and south of this boundary the combination of strong shear and strong instability will be sufficient to support supercells with long track, intense tornadoes. We will be monitoring this warm sector from here on out for convective initiation. Confidence is high for severe storms to also develop along the dry line in West TX and threaten western OK and western North Texas late this afternoon and evening. In summary, the shear and instability in the warm sector is unusually favorable for intense tornadoes. This will be a protracted period of threat, lasting into the overnight hours. We are also dedicating extra resources to monitor the developing hydrologic situation. Exceptionally high rainfall rates in will result in significant and potentially life threatening flash flooding. It's important this message not be lost in the overall concern over tornadoes. This factor needs to be considered as sheltering plans are made. Additional updates will follow this afternoon.

column9: Today (Monday) is a day that you need to pay VERY close attention to the weather if you are in Oklahoma or north Texas, especially in western Oklahoma and adjacent parts of Texas. We expect storms to begin this morning as potential hail producers. While these storms may produce severe hail (1 inch diameter or more), they will most likely be only marginally severe at worst. Around noon, the scenario changes. Storms are expected to take on supercell structures, and such storms can produce very large hail, very damaging winds, and tornadoes. This risk will begin initially across western Oklahoma and Texas, then expand quickly east through the afternoon, and continue well into the evening. By late evening and overnight, storms are expected to merge into a large area, and will mainly pose a risk of flooding (possibly serious flooding) and strong winds. Hail and tornadoes will still be possible, but not as likely as in the afternoon and evening.The storms are expected to clear from west to east overnight, finally becoming non-severe or east of our forecast area sometime Tuesday morning. Additional severe weather will be possible again Wednesday and Thursday, but the extent and magnitude of the storms those days are expected to be less than today's.Have a plan, and use it if severe weather threatens your location.

We don't know for sure if we'll have tornadoes, how bad they might be if they happen and who they might affect. All we can do right now is make sure we are as ready as we can be for whatever ends up happening. If the forecast is causing you fear, stress or anxiety, try to think about the things you can do to empower yourself. We can't stop the storms, but you can take charge of those things that you have control over: - Figure out where you will take shelter if there's a tornado. Decide today and be sure your shelter is ready. - Make sure your family and friends are aware of the chance of bad storms Monday. Some people don't pay close attention to the weather over the weekend.- Pay close attention to the forecast, especially starting early Monday morning. column9: 5:50 PM - here's a technical update on the continuing severe weather potential across southwest Oklahoma. This event is NOT over! SUMMARY...The severe threat continues across WW 199. A volatile environment remains in place across the discussion area with all modes of severe (including significant tornadoes) remaining possible. DISCUSSION...In the short term, tornado potential appears to be maximized in a couple of areas - one over Greer County, OK (where recent radar trends indicate potential for significant tornadoes and very large hail) and near Noble/Payne Counties in OK where a forward-propagating linear segment may interact with an outflow/warm frontal boundary immediately downstream of that region. Surface-based storms continue in a very volatile shear/instability combination, with all modes of severe remaining possible (including significant tornadoes). Shear will only increase in response to significant strengthening of low-level flow through the evening. A convectively modified surface boundary continues to migrate slowly southward across west-central Oklahoma and resides along a line from near PNC to just south of CSM and westward to south of AMA. Storms north of this boundary will be elevated, but capable of large hail. If the current storm near Greer County, OK can continue on the warm side of the boundary, it will continue with a risk of occasional strong to violent tornadogenesis in addition to large hail and damaging wind gusts.

We have high confidence that severe weather will affect parts of SE LA and S MS tomorrow, with the greatest likelihood across areas that are generally along/north of a line from Baton Rouge to McComb.

* Damaging wind gusts in excess of 60 mph, which could down trees and powerlines, and cause minor structural damage
* Tornadoes, a few of which could be strong and/or long track mainly in the enhanced risk area
* Large hail greater than 1" in diameter
Safety steps you can take now:
* Monitor the forecast for any changes - especially changes in timing
* Plan ahead - have multiple ways to receive warnings, and know where your safe place will be if any warnings are issued for your area.

Here's the latest update on the severe weather threat today and tonight. 
Severe weather is likely late this afternoon through tonight across Southeast Louisiana and Southern Mississippi. While all of the area will have some threat, the greatest threat will generally be along and north of a line from Lafayette to Hammond to Hattiesburg.
The timing of storms is generally expected to begin during the late afternoon and progress eastward through the evening and overnight hours. The threat should be over across our Mississippi Coastal counties before daybreak Sunday.
The threats associated with today's severe weather will be:
* Tornadoes - some of which could be strong and/or long tracked across areas from Lafayette to Hammond to Hattiesburg and northward.
* Wind gusts in excess of 60 mph which can down trees and power lines, and cause minor structural damage
* Large hail
Preparedness:
* Make sure you have multiple ways to receive warnings
* Know where your safe shelter will be if a warning is issued for your area
* Remember, mobile homes are not safe during tornadoes even if they are tied down. If you live in a mobile home, have a plan to be in a safer location during the severe weather timing.

column9:
Middle Tennessee is expecting a lot of rainfall from Tuesday through at least the upcoming weekend. There could be concerns that some area roadways, especially secondary ones, at particular locations could be covered with unknown depth of water.  We have a saying here at the National Weather Service (NWS) Office in Nashville concerning this:  When Flooded Turn Around Don't Drown.  It is very important to remember that to never drive around the barriers blocking a flooded road!  The road may have collapsed under that water.  A mere 6 inches of fast-moving flood water can knock over an adult.  It takes just 12 inches of rushing water to carry away most cars and just 2 feet of rushing water can carry away SUVs and trucks.  It is NEVER safe to drive or walk into flood waters!  There is an excellent Public Service Announcement (PSA) by Matt Hawk concerning this.  To access this PSA and for further information too, visit the Turn Around Don't Drown Website: http://ow.ly/hfML30nJyPl.  This website is a sub website of a much larger website concerning NWS Flood Safety and Resources: http://ow.ly/cF8B30nJyVf.
Do you want to ask a NWS Meteorologist a question in person?  Please come to Severe Weather Awareness Day, Saturday, March 2nd, 2019, 9 am - 4 pm, Trevecca Nazarene University Boone Business Building, in Nashville: http://ow.ly/mYCn30nJySO

column9:
So all that and no storms? What happened?
We had all the ingredients we needed in abudance: moisture, heating, instability, increasing winds above the surface. We knew we would have all these severe thunderstorm ingredients at the ready today.
-----
Well then, why no storms?
We anticipated storms to focus along the dry line, a boundary between very dry air & very moist air. The dry line moved across MO as expected but we didn't have enough air colliding at the surface to rise and form thunderstorms!
-----
Sometimes that's all it takes, one missing ingredient and the day looks completely different than what we expected.   
-------
Take aways from today: are you prepared for the day we do have all the thunderstorm ingredients in place? 
-Have a way to get warnings, even at night
-Have a weather safety plan
-Know when to put your safety plan into action
#stlwx #mowx #ilwx #midmowx

So all that and no storms? What happened?
We had all the ingredients we needed in abudance: moisture, heating, instability, increasing winds above the surface. We knew we would have all these severe thunderstorm ingredients at the ready today.
-----
Well then, why no storms?
We anticipated storms to focus along the dry line, a boundary between very dry air & very moist air. The dry line moved across MO as expected but we didn't have enough air colliding at the surface to rise and form thunderstorms!
-----
Sometimes that's all it takes, one missing ingredient and the day looks completely different than what we expected.   
-------
Take aways from today: are you prepared for the day we do have all the thunderstorm ingredients in place? 
-Have a way to get warnings, even at night
-Have a weather safety plan
-Know when to put your safety plan into action
#stlwx #mowx #ilwx #midmowx

column9: We have had questions about the PDS wording in the Tornado Watch and what it means. Here is the definition from The Storm Prediction Center... The "Particularly Dangerous Situation" wording is used in Tornado Watches for rare situations when long-lived intense tornadoes are likely. This enhanced wording may also accompany Severe Thunderstorm Watches for widespread significant severe events, usually produced by exceptionally intense derechos. PDS watches are issued, when in the opinion of the forecaster, the likelihood of significant events is boosted by very volatile atmospheric conditions. Usually this decision is based on a number of atmospheric clues and parameters, so the decision to issue a PDS watch is subjective with no hard criteria.

column9: A very strong warm front is becoming anchored across south-central Alabama westward across south-central Mississippi.  Temperatures and dewpoints to the north of the warm front are currently in the upper 50s, while just south temperatures are nearing 80 degrees with dewpoints in the lower 70s.  Numerous showers and thunderstorms have developed on the cold side of this boundary and should not allow it to move much further north in the near term.  An outflow boundary which moved south from the earlier storms in central Alabama is aligned south of the warm front and has become a recent focus for new storm development over Butler, Crenshaw, and Covington counties, AL.  These storms are being monitored closely and may gradually intensify and result in a short-term severe risk as instability and shear are increasing.  Overall threat in these areas should be damaging winds, as low level winds remain southwesterly.  Further west, the atmosphere continues to rapidly destabilize with strong daytime heating as low clouds have broken and will continue to break up over southeast Mississippi into southwest Alabama.   This should result in strong thermodynamic instability and shear/helicity is also increasing with low level winds aligned more southerly.  The latest morning soundings suggest that this atmosphere remains capped by an inversion.  As strong heating continues and modest height falls spread east with the approaching upper level disturbance this afternoon, storms may erupt over portions of the warm sector and storm mode would be supercells.  This will be especially true in the vicinity of the warm front stretched over northern areas.  This threat should evolve by early to mid afternoon and continue through the evening hours with all modes of severe weather possible, including tornadoes (some which may be strong), large hail to golf ball size or greater, and damaging winds potentially in excess of 70 mph.  This will be especially true with any supercells that can evolve over the warm sector or on the warm front.  NWS New Orleans will be launching another weather balloon at noon, so we will have a better idea of how the atmosphere is changing and will provide an update.  A tornado watch will be likely by early to mid afternoon for portions of our area.  Please continue to closely monitor this evolving severe weather threat.  - NWS Mobile

column9: A very strong warm front is becoming anchored across south-central Alabama westward across south-central Mississippi.  Temperatures and dewpoints to the north of the warm front are currently in the upper 50s, while just south temperatures are nearing 80 degrees with dewpoints in the lower 70s.  Numerous showers and thunderstorms have developed on the cold side of this boundary and should not allow it to move much further north in the near term.  An outflow boundary which moved south from the earlier storms in central Alabama is aligned south of the warm front and has become a recent focus for new storm development over Butler, Crenshaw, and Covington counties, AL.  These storms are being monitored closely and may gradually intensify and result in a short-term severe risk as instability and shear are increasing.  Overall threat in these areas should be damaging winds, as low level winds remain southwesterly.  Further west, the atmosphere continues to rapidly destabilize with strong daytime heating as low clouds have broken and will continue to break up over southeast Mississippi into southwest Alabama.   This should result in strong thermodynamic instability and shear/helicity is also increasing with low level winds aligned more southerly.  The latest morning soundings suggest that this atmosphere remains capped by an inversion.  As strong heating continues and modest height falls spread east with the approaching upper level disturbance this afternoon, storms may erupt over portions of the warm sector and storm mode would be supercells.  This will be especially true in the vicinity of the warm front stretched over northern areas.  This threat should evolve by early to mid afternoon and continue through the evening hours with all modes of severe weather possible, including tornadoes (some which may be strong), large hail to golf ball size or greater, and damaging winds potentially in excess of 70 mph.  This will be especially true with any supercells that can evolve over the warm sector or on the warm front.  NWS New Orleans will be launching another weather balloon at noon, so we will have a better idea of how the atmosphere is changing and will provide an update.  A tornado watch will be likely by early to mid afternoon for portions of our area.  Please continue to closely monitor this evolving severe weather threat.  - NWS Mobile

column9: A very strong warm front is becoming anchored across south-central Alabama westward across south-central Mississippi.  Temperatures and dewpoints to the north of the warm front are currently in the upper 50s, while just south temperatures are nearing 80 degrees with dewpoints in the lower 70s.  Numerous showers and thunderstorms have developed on the cold side of this boundary and should not allow it to move much further north in the near term.  An outflow boundary which moved south from the earlier storms in central Alabama is aligned south of the warm front and has become a recent focus for new storm development over Butler, Crenshaw, and Covington counties, AL.  These storms are being monitored closely and may gradually intensify and result in a short-term severe risk as instability and shear are increasing.  Overall threat in these areas should be damaging winds, as low level winds remain southwesterly.  Further west, the atmosphere continues to rapidly destabilize with strong daytime heating as low clouds have broken and will continue to break up over southeast Mississippi into southwest Alabama.   This should result in strong thermodynamic instability and shear/helicity is also increasing with low level winds aligned more southerly.  The latest morning soundings suggest that this atmosphere remains capped by an inversion.  As strong heating continues and modest height falls spread east with the approaching upper level disturbance this afternoon, storms may erupt over portions of the warm sector and storm mode would be supercells.  This will be especially true in the vicinity of the warm front stretched over northern areas.  This threat should evolve by early to mid afternoon and continue through the evening hours with all modes of severe weather possible, including tornadoes (some which may be strong), large hail to golf ball size or greater, and damaging winds potentially in excess of 70 mph.  This will be especially true with any supercells that can evolve over the warm sector or on the warm front.  NWS New Orleans will be launching another weather balloon at noon, so we will have a better idea of how the atmosphere is changing and will provide an update.  A tornado watch will be likely by early to mid afternoon for portions of our area.  Please continue to closely monitor this evolving severe weather threat.  - NWS Mobile

Heavy rainfall with some of these storms may also produce a additional hazard of flooding. There is the potential for another round of severe storms on Monday (tomorrow) and will finally get out of this large scale wet system by mid-week. However, another couple of smaller scale weather disturbances off the higher plains may come through toward the end of the week, with additional but for now low chances of storms.

📢 Attention!! Tornadic Storms Possible Today!! Please share this with as many people as possible 📢
That's a headline everyone knew already, right?
SPC issued a "High" risk over portions of southwest Middle TN this morning (putting most of the rest of the mid-state in a Moderate), but it doesn't change much in the way of our thinking:
1. Non-severe showers and thunderstorms have already moved into southern portions of Middle TN. These will spread northward through the morning and (we expect) these to come to an end by late morning.
2. The first of two potential rounds of severe weather starts this afternoon around 1 pm CDT. This first round hinges on whether the rains last longer than expected. If they stick around until mid-afternoon (which we don't expect), this will reduce the likelihood of afternoon severe weather. However, if they end and the sun comes out, this will only act to enhance the severe weather threat between 1 pm and about 6 pm this afternoon. If these storms start to develop, this is when we could see the stronger, long-track tornadoes occur. The best location for this to occur is south of I-40 and west of I-65. Large hail and localized flash flooding is also possible.
3. The second round is expected between 6 pm and 11 pm CDT. This would consist of a broken line of intense thunderstorms that will present the possibility of damaging straight line winds (65+ mph), multiple tornadoes and flash flooding and these threats will be for ALL of Middle TN.
Key takeaways:
- Confidence on the afternoon storms occurring is low to medium. Lots of things have to come together for this to happen. On the other hand, confidence on the evening broken line of storms is higher.
- If you have outdoor plans today, the best bet is to postpone. However, if you must push forward, please remain extremely weather aware and
- Have shelter readily available. If it isn’t (i.e. a mobile home), consider spending the afternoon/evening some place where it is.
- Shelter in place as soon as a warning is issued. Do not venture outside.
- DO NOT ignore Severe Thunderstorm Warnings issued for your area. Treat them the same as you would a Tornado Warning.
On a personal note, I was intimately involved with the April 27, 2011 outbreak across the south; forecasting, issuing warnings and damage surveys for the following week. Please take this seriously. I haven't seen severe weather parameters like we're seeing for today since then. Statistically speaking, you won't be affected by the storms today, but I don't want anyone to become a statistic. Just take shelter if you go under a warning. We don't need videos or pictures. We just want everyone to be safe.
Keep an eye on our Facebook feed as we'll likely do another Facebook LIVE update later this morning to give you the latest information.

That's a headline everyone knew already, right?
SPC issued a "High" risk over portions of southwest Middle TN this morning (putting most of the rest of the mid-state in a Moderate), but it doesn't change much in the way of our thinking:
1. Non-severe showers and thunderstorms have already moved into southern portions of Middle TN. These will spread northward through the morning and (we expect) these to come to an end by late morning.
2. The first of two potential rounds of severe weather starts this afternoon around 1 pm CDT. This first round hinges on whether the rains last longer than expected. If they stick around until mid-afternoon (which we don't expect), this will reduce the likelihood of afternoon severe weather. However, if they end and the sun comes out, this will only act to enhance the severe weather threat between 1 pm and about 6 pm this afternoon. If these storms start to develop, this is when we could see the stronger, long-track tornadoes occur. The best location for this to occur is south of I-40 and west of I-65. Large hail and localized flash flooding is also possible.
3. The second round is expected between 6 pm and 11 pm CDT. This would consist of a broken line of intense thunderstorms that will present the possibility of damaging straight line winds (65+ mph), multiple tornadoes and flash flooding and these threats will be for ALL of Middle TN.
Key takeaways:
- Confidence on the afternoon storms occurring is low to medium. Lots of things have to come together for this to happen. On the other hand, confidence on the evening broken line of storms is higher.
- If you have outdoor plans today, the best bet is to postpone. However, if you must push forward, please remain extremely weather aware and
- Have shelter readily available. If it isn’t (i.e. a mobile home), consider spending the afternoon/evening some place where it is.
- Shelter in place as soon as a warning is issued. Do not venture outside.
- DO NOT ignore Severe Thunderstorm Warnings issued for your area. Treat them the same as you would a Tornado Warning.
On a personal note, I was intimately involved with the April 27, 2011 outbreak across the south; forecasting, issuing warnings and damage surveys for the following week. Please take this seriously. I haven't seen severe weather parameters like we're seeing for today since then. Statistically speaking, you won't be affected by the storms today, but I don't want anyone to become a statistic. Just take shelter if you go under a warning. We don't need videos or pictures. We just want everyone to be safe.
Keep an eye on our Facebook feed as we'll likely do another Facebook LIVE update later this morning to give you the latest information.

📢 Attention!! Tornadic Storms Possible Today!! Please share this with as many people as possible 📢
That's a headline everyone knew already, right?
SPC issued a "High" risk over portions of southwest Middle TN this morning (putting most of the rest of the mid-state in a Moderate), but it doesn't change much in the way of our thinking:
1. Non-severe showers and thunderstorms have already moved into southern portions of Middle TN. These will spread northward through the morning and (we expect) these to come to an end by late morning.
2. The first of two potential rounds of severe weather starts this afternoon around 1 pm CDT. This first round hinges on whether the rains last longer than expected. If they stick around until mid-afternoon (which we don't expect), this will reduce the likelihood of afternoon severe weather. However, if they end and the sun comes out, this will only act to enhance the severe weather threat between 1 pm and about 6 pm this afternoon. If these storms start to develop, this is when we could see the stronger, long-track tornadoes occur. The best location for this to occur is south of I-40 and west of I-65. Large hail and localized flash flooding is also possible.
3. The second round is expected between 6 pm and 11 pm CDT. This would consist of a broken line of intense thunderstorms that will present the possibility of damaging straight line winds (65+ mph), multiple tornadoes and flash flooding and these threats will be for ALL of Middle TN.
Key takeaways:
- Confidence on the afternoon storms occurring is low to medium. Lots of things have to come together for this to happen. On the other hand, confidence on the evening broken line of storms is higher.
- If you have outdoor plans today, the best bet is to postpone. However, if you must push forward, please remain extremely weather aware and
- Have shelter readily available. If it isn’t (i.e. a mobile home), consider spending the afternoon/evening some place where it is.
- Shelter in place as soon as a warning is issued. Do not venture outside.
- DO NOT ignore Severe Thunderstorm Warnings issued for your area. Treat them the same as you would a Tornado Warning.
On a personal note, I was intimately involved with the April 27, 2011 outbreak across the south; forecasting, issuing warnings and damage surveys for the following week. Please take this seriously. I haven't seen severe weather parameters like we're seeing for today since then. Statistically speaking, you won't be affected by the storms today, but I don't want anyone to become a statistic. Just take shelter if you go under a warning. We don't need videos or pictures. We just want everyone to be safe.
Keep an eye on our Facebook feed as we'll likely do another Facebook LIVE update later this morning to give you the latest information.

📢 Attention!! Tornadic Storms Possible Today!! Please share this with as many people as possible 📢
That's a headline everyone knew already, right?
SPC issued a "High" risk over portions of southwest Middle TN this morning (putting most of the rest of the mid-state in a Moderate), but it doesn't change much in the way of our thinking:
1. Non-severe showers and thunderstorms have already moved into southern portions of Middle TN. These will spread northward through the morning and (we expect) these to come to an end by late morning.
2. The first of two potential rounds of severe weather starts this afternoon around 1 pm CDT. This first round hinges on whether the rains last longer than expected. If they stick around until mid-afternoon (which we don't expect), this will reduce the likelihood of afternoon severe weather. However, if they end and the sun comes out, this will only act to enhance the severe weather threat between 1 pm and about 6 pm this afternoon. If these storms start to develop, this is when we could see the stronger, long-track tornadoes occur. The best location for this to occur is south of I-40 and west of I-65. Large hail and localized flash flooding is also possible.
3. The second round is expected between 6 pm and 11 pm CDT. This would consist of a broken line of intense thunderstorms that will present the possibility of damaging straight line winds (65+ mph), multiple tornadoes and flash flooding and these threats will be for ALL of Middle TN.
Key takeaways:
- Confidence on the afternoon storms occurring is low to medium. Lots of things have to come together for this to happen. On the other hand, confidence on the evening broken line of storms is higher.
- If you have outdoor plans today, the best bet is to postpone. However, if you must push forward, please remain extremely weather aware and
- Have shelter readily available. If it isn’t (i.e. a mobile home), consider spending the afternoon/evening some place where it is.
- Shelter in place as soon as a warning is issued. Do not venture outside.
- DO NOT ignore Severe Thunderstorm Warnings issued for your area. Treat them the same as you would a Tornado Warning.
On a personal note, I was intimately involved with the April 27, 2011 outbreak across the south; forecasting, issuing warnings and damage surveys for the following week. Please take this seriously. I haven't seen severe weather parameters like we're seeing for today since then. Statistically speaking, you won't be affected by the storms today, but I don't want anyone to become a statistic. Just take shelter if you go under a warning. We don't need videos or pictures. We just want everyone to be safe.
Keep an eye on our Facebook feed as we'll likely do another Facebook LIVE update later this morning to give you the latest information.

📢 Attention!! Tornadic Storms Possible Today!! Please share this with as many people as possible 📢
That's a headline everyone knew already, right?
SPC issued a "High" risk over portions of southwest Middle TN this morning (putting most of the rest of the mid-state in a Moderate), but it doesn't change much in the way of our thinking:
1. Non-severe showers and thunderstorms have already moved into southern portions of Middle TN. These will spread northward through the morning and (we expect) these to come to an end by late morning.
2. The first of two potential rounds of severe weather starts this afternoon around 1 pm CDT. This first round hinges on whether the rains last longer than expected. If they stick around until mid-afternoon (which we don't expect), this will reduce the likelihood of afternoon severe weather. However, if they end and the sun comes out, this will only act to enhance the severe weather threat between 1 pm and about 6 pm this afternoon. If these storms start to develop, this is when we could see the stronger, long-track tornadoes occur. The best location for this to occur is south of I-40 and west of I-65. Large hail and localized flash flooding is also possible.
3. The second round is expected between 6 pm and 11 pm CDT. This would consist of a broken line of intense thunderstorms that will present the possibility of damaging straight line winds (65+ mph), multiple tornadoes and flash flooding and these threats will be for ALL of Middle TN.
Key takeaways:
- Confidence on the afternoon storms occurring is low to medium. Lots of things have to come together for this to happen. On the other hand, confidence on the evening broken line of storms is higher.
- If you have outdoor plans today, the best bet is to postpone. However, if you must push forward, please remain extremely weather aware and
- Have shelter readily available. If it isn’t (i.e. a mobile home), consider spending the afternoon/evening some place where it is.
- Shelter in place as soon as a warning is issued. Do not venture outside.
- DO NOT ignore Severe Thunderstorm Warnings issued for your area. Treat them the same as you would a Tornado Warning.
On a personal note, I was intimately involved with the April 27, 2011 outbreak across the south; forecasting, issuing warnings and damage surveys for the following week. Please take this seriously. I haven't seen severe weather parameters like we're seeing for today since then. Statistically speaking, you won't be affected by the storms today, but I don't want anyone to become a statistic. Just take shelter if you go under a warning. We don't need videos or pictures. We just want everyone to be safe.
Keep an eye on our Facebook feed as we'll likely do another Facebook LIVE update later this morning to give you the latest information.

column9:
Aaah...spring time in Middle TN. Flowers blooming, warmer temperatures and......severe weather.
Yep. Confidence has increased over the last 24 hours that we'll have another shot at severe weather in the afternoon and early evening Thursday (3/25). All modes of severe weather will be possible and while damaging straight line winds are still the biggest concern, it does look like there will be a tornado threat, especially south of I-40 and west of I-24.
What's different this time, you ask? We didn't get anything last week. Well, this scenario looks different. We got long-lasting rain in the morning and it stabilized the atmosphere to the point where severe storms couldn't develop. Models do show morning showers along the warm front as it pulls into Middle TN tomorrow morning, but nothing like last week. This means the atmosphere will have the opportunity to destabilize so storms can form.
The main time frame for this severe weather currently looks like 2 pm to 10 pm Thursday. This could be adjusted by an hour or two as we're still 24+ hours out, but this should be a good approximation.
Bottom line: it's still not time to panic. Take the time today to do 2 things.
1. Make sure you have multiple ways to get warnings, be it NOAA Weather Radio and/or an app on your phone. While you're doing that, check the batteries in your NOAA Weather Radio and make sure they're fresh. We will run a weather radio test today between 11 am and noon CDT.
2. Review your safety plan with your family. Know how and where to go in the event you go under a warning. Where is your shelter? Don't have a safety plan? Visit ready.gov/plan for pointers.
Planning ahead for severe weather reduces the stress you might experience once you go under a warning.
We'll update you a few more times before storms start to develop on Thursday so you have the latest, most up-to-date information.

If you took 10 min last week to prepare, that's great! Now you can do it again. If you didn't, it's not too late to start. Get those safety kits ready, figure out a safe place to go, make sure you have more than one or two ways to receive warnings, check in with family and friends and make sure they are ready, and keep an eye on what is happening throughout the day. We're ready here at the NWS. Our families are ready. Are you?

Aaah...spring time in Middle TN. Flowers blooming, warmer temperatures and......severe weather.
Yep. Confidence has increased over the last 24 hours that we'll have another shot at severe weather in the afternoon and early evening Thursday (3/25). All modes of severe weather will be possible and while damaging straight line winds are still the biggest concern, it does look like there will be a tornado threat, especially south of I-40 and west of I-24.
What's different this time, you ask? We didn't get anything last week. Well, this scenario looks different. We got long-lasting rain in the morning and it stabilized the atmosphere to the point where severe storms couldn't develop. Models do show morning showers along the warm front as it pulls into Middle TN tomorrow morning, but nothing like last week. This means the atmosphere will have the opportunity to destabilize so storms can form.
The main time frame for this severe weather currently looks like 2 pm to 10 pm Thursday. This could be adjusted by an hour or two as we're still 24+ hours out, but this should be a good approximation.
Bottom line: it's still not time to panic. Take the time today to do 2 things.
1. Make sure you have multiple ways to get warnings, be it NOAA Weather Radio and/or an app on your phone. While you're doing that, check the batteries in your NOAA Weather Radio and make sure they're fresh. We will run a weather radio test today between 11 am and noon CDT.
2. Review your safety plan with your family. Know how and where to go in the event you go under a warning. Where is your shelter? Don't have a safety plan? Visit ready.gov/plan for pointers.
Planning ahead for severe weather reduces the stress you might experience once you go under a warning.
We'll update you a few more times before storms start to develop on Thursday so you have the latest, most up-to-date information.

That's a headline everyone knew already, right?
SPC issued a "High" risk over portions of southwest Middle TN this morning (putting most of the rest of the mid-state in a Moderate), but it doesn't change much in the way of our thinking:
1. Non-severe showers and thunderstorms have already moved into southern portions of Middle TN. These will spread northward through the morning and (we expect) these to come to an end by late morning.
2. The first of two potential rounds of severe weather starts this afternoon around 1 pm CDT. This first round hinges on whether the rains last longer than expected. If they stick around until mid-afternoon (which we don't expect), this will reduce the likelihood of afternoon severe weather. However, if they end and the sun comes out, this will only act to enhance the severe weather threat between 1 pm and about 6 pm this afternoon. If these storms start to develop, this is when we could see the stronger, long-track tornadoes occur. The best location for this to occur is south of I-40 and west of I-65. Large hail and localized flash flooding is also possible.
3. The second round is expected between 6 pm and 11 pm CDT. This would consist of a broken line of intense thunderstorms that will present the possibility of damaging straight line winds (65+ mph), multiple tornadoes and flash flooding and these threats will be for ALL of Middle TN.
Key takeaways:
- Confidence on the afternoon storms occurring is low to medium. Lots of things have to come together for this to happen. On the other hand, confidence on the evening broken line of storms is higher.
- If you have outdoor plans today, the best bet is to postpone. However, if you must push forward, please remain extremely weather aware and
- Have shelter readily available. If it isn’t (i.e. a mobile home), consider spending the afternoon/evening some place where it is.
- Shelter in place as soon as a warning is issued. Do not venture outside.
- DO NOT ignore Severe Thunderstorm Warnings issued for your area. Treat them the same as you would a Tornado Warning.
On a personal note, I was intimately involved with the April 27, 2011 outbreak across the south; forecasting, issuing warnings and damage surveys for the following week. Please take this seriously. I haven't seen severe weather parameters like we're seeing for today since then. Statistically speaking, you won't be affected by the storms today, but I don't want anyone to become a statistic. Just take shelter if you go under a warning. We don't need videos or pictures. We just want everyone to be safe.
Keep an eye on our Facebook feed as we'll likely do another Facebook LIVE update later this morning to give you the latest information.

We know we just went through a day with severe weather last week, and it's tiring to hear about going through another one again today. Believe me, we KNOW. 
But don't let your guard down today. High and moderate risks are not issued because someone "feels" like it. There is a reason. Shear is there, instability is there, moisture, lift, it's all there. Will they work out just right and give us those strong and terrible storms? Well, we'll see. But all the ingredients are there to do just that. 
If you took 10 min last week to prepare, that's great! Now you can do it again. If you didn't, it's not too late to start. Get those safety kits ready, figure out a safe place to go, make sure you have more than one or two ways to receive warnings, check in with family and friends and make sure they are ready, and keep an eye on what is happening throughout the day. We're ready here at the NWS. Our families are ready. Are you?

That's a headline everyone knew already, right?
SPC issued a "High" risk over portions of southwest Middle TN this morning (putting most of the rest of the mid-state in a Moderate), but it doesn't change much in the way of our thinking:
1. Non-severe showers and thunderstorms have already moved into southern portions of Middle TN. These will spread northward through the morning and (we expect) these to come to an end by late morning.
2. The first of two potential rounds of severe weather starts this afternoon around 1 pm CDT. This first round hinges on whether the rains last longer than expected. If they stick around until mid-afternoon (which we don't expect), this will reduce the likelihood of afternoon severe weather. However, if they end and the sun comes out, this will only act to enhance the severe weather threat between 1 pm and about 6 pm this afternoon. If these storms start to develop, this is when we could see the stronger, long-track tornadoes occur. The best location for this to occur is south of I-40 and west of I-65. Large hail and localized flash flooding is also possible.
3. The second round is expected between 6 pm and 11 pm CDT. This would consist of a broken line of intense thunderstorms that will present the possibility of damaging straight line winds (65+ mph), multiple tornadoes and flash flooding and these threats will be for ALL of Middle TN.
Key takeaways:
- Confidence on the afternoon storms occurring is low to medium. Lots of things have to come together for this to happen. On the other hand, confidence on the evening broken line of storms is higher.
- If you have outdoor plans today, the best bet is to postpone. However, if you must push forward, please remain extremely weather aware and
- Have shelter readily available. If it isn’t (i.e. a mobile home), consider spending the afternoon/evening some place where it is.
- Shelter in place as soon as a warning is issued. Do not venture outside.
- DO NOT ignore Severe Thunderstorm Warnings issued for your area. Treat them the same as you would a Tornado Warning.
On a personal note, I was intimately involved with the April 27, 2011 outbreak across the south; forecasting, issuing warnings and damage surveys for the following week. Please take this seriously. I haven't seen severe weather parameters like we're seeing for today since then. Statistically speaking, you won't be affected by the storms today, but I don't want anyone to become a statistic. Please pay attention and prepare to seek shelter if Severe Thunderstorm Warnings are issued for your location. Damaging winds can be more damaging than tornadoes in some cases, especially when it comes to the extent of areas impacted.
Prepare now for nighttime severe weather across the state!

Potential Timing for Tuesday Night Severe Weather
We all know that timing is critical when preparing for severe weather. The main timeframe for severe weather Tuesday into Tuesday night will be from 7-8 PM across northwest Arkansas to roughly 4 AM across southeast Arkansas.
Storms will enter NW portions of the state first, then make their way southeastward and impact much of the state. Some hail is possible along with the potential for a few tornadoes (mainly across western Arkansas) but THE PRIMARY THREAT WITH TONIGHT'S THUNDERSORMS WILL BE DAMAGING WINDS! This means that winds in excess of 60-70 mph will be possible across a large portion of the state with some locations potentially seeing even higher wind speeds!
Please pay attention and prepare to seek shelter if Severe Thunderstorm Warnings are issued for your location. Damaging winds can be more damaging than tornadoes in some cases, especially when it comes to the extent of areas impacted.
Prepare now for nighttime severe weather across the state!

7:00 PM - here's a technical update about the developing situation. If you want to skip the technical details, here's a summary:
- Storms that will eventually have the potential to produce tornadoes are increasing across western Oklahoma. The tornado threat will be highest for the next few hours.
- When storms eventually form into a line, there will still be a risk of some weaker very brief tornadoes. 
Now the gory details:
Quick update on the mesoscale environment. Radar shows the boundary now extends from near Blackwell to Pond Creek to Waynoka to just south of Buffalo, and continues to slowly drift south. Storm coverage is greatest north of the boundary and the primary hazard will be heavy rainfall/flooding and large hail with these storms. 
Further south, surface based discrete storms are increasing across western Oklahoma and the eastern Texas Panhandle. As low-level shear gradually trends upward, the tornado threat will increase. The best window for tornadoes should begin in the next hour or so and continue until upscale growth occurs and discrete modes lessen. 
Once this happens, we'll have to watch for QLCS tornado potential. But, the 0-3-km shear magnitude and orientation isn't the most favorable for QLCS tornadoes. The best chance of one happening would be near local surges/rear-inflow jets or segments of the line that can become oriented more northwest to southeast.

What's with the wide time window? Let's look...
there will basically be two "waves" of storms today through tomorrow. The first, highlighted in yellow, is a scattered area of storms moving roughly northeast. This will be the main cause of severe weather this afternoon and early evening. The second "wave" highlighted in red, is closer to the front and will be moving through overnight into the morning Thursday. The area in red has scattered storms showing on radar, but all of these storms are expected to merge into a line feature sometime right before entering Alabama. This is what will cause the main focus of severe weather through the overnight hours. 
To add to this explanation, a big uncertainty is how quickly that area in red will move through. If it moves quickly, the atmosphere may not have time to recover from the first wave (remember, the one in yellow), and we may not see quite as much severe weather. If it moves slowly, the atmosphere will have time to gather more energy, and we may have a greater severe weather threat.

column9: Wednesday severe storm threat (Tuesday AM Update): The severe threat has increased for the southwest portion of the mid state as of this morning. Unfortunately that means the threat of damaging winds, large hail, flash flooding, and even tornadoes has increased mainly for the southwest, but again, everyone in the mid state needs to remain weather aware for Wednesday. From yesterday's post, we mentioned the position of the warm front will have the greatest impact on the environment Wednesday afternoon and evening, and that remains true. Models want to bring the warm front into the area oriented along I-24 (with the warmest and most unstable air south and west of I-24 in the Slight/Enhanced/Marginal Risk areas) Wednesday afternoon. But, if that front moves further north and east, the severe threat will spread north and east with it. Now is the time to start making plans for Wednesday afternoon and evening. Have multiple ways to get warnings and keep your cell phones on as the severe threat will persist into the evening and possibly into the overnight hours early Thursday morning. Damaging wind gusts remain the primary threat with any severe thunderstorms that develop, but large hail, flooding, and a few tornadoes will all be possible. Stay tuned for updates and any changes to the forecast for Wednesday!

column9: You have may have seen this graphic in many forms today, and you probably have questions about what it means.  This graphic is depicting the likelihood of seeing severe weather in different parts of the area, with the highest likelihood being across the red ("moderate risk") area and the lower likelihood being in the green ("marginal risk").  BUT this doesn't tell you the whole story, and there are some important things you need to be aware of.It has been pointed out that last year's devastating tornadoes that hit Nashville and Cookeville occurred in a green/marginal risk threat area. Why did this happen? Because the conditions that night were "marginal" for tornadoes: We had very strong winds in place, but the atmospheric energy that is needed for strong storms was barely there. 9 times out of 10 this combination of strong winds and low atmospheric energy leads to either weak/brief tornadoes or none at all. Last year's storms were the exception to this rule, and proof that just because a risk is LOW does not mean it is ZERO. So what does this mean for tonight? If you are in the yellow or dark green area, you are once again looking at conditions that are not extremely favorable for strong tornadoes, yet they can't be ruled out. Those conditions get more favorable in the orange ("enhanced") area, and very favorable further south across MS and AL.  However just because you are in a lower risk area, it doesn't mean you are in a zero risk area, and for this reason we want EVERYONE to treat tonight's storm threat seriously. Don't worry about where you are on this map, just be sure you are ready to take action in case we issue a warning for your area.

column9: Wednesday severe storm threat (Tuesday AM Update): The severe threat has increased for the southwest portion of the mid state as of this morning. Unfortunately that means the threat of damaging winds, large hail, flash flooding, and even tornadoes has increased mainly for the southwest, but again, everyone in the mid state needs to remain weather aware for Wednesday. From yesterday's post, we mentioned the position of the warm front will have the greatest impact on the environment Wednesday afternoon and evening, and that remains true. Models want to bring the warm front into the area oriented along I-24 (with the warmest and most unstable air south and west of I-24 in the Slight/Enhanced/Marginal Risk areas) Wednesday afternoon. But, if that front moves further north and east, the severe threat will spread north and east with it. Now is the time to start making plans for Wednesday afternoon and evening. Have multiple ways to get warnings and keep your cell phones on as the severe threat will persist into the evening and possibly into the overnight hours early Thursday morning. Damaging wind gusts remain the primary threat with any severe thunderstorms that develop, but large hail, flooding, and a few tornadoes will all be possible. Stay tuned for updates and any changes to the forecast for Wednesday!

column9: Wednesday severe storm threat (Tuesday AM Update): The severe threat has increased for the southwest portion of the mid state as of this morning. Unfortunately that means the threat of damaging winds, large hail, flash flooding, and even tornadoes has increased mainly for the southwest, but again, everyone in the mid state needs to remain weather aware for Wednesday. From yesterday's post, we mentioned the position of the warm front will have the greatest impact on the environment Wednesday afternoon and evening, and that remains true. Models want to bring the warm front into the area oriented along I-24 (with the warmest and most unstable air south and west of I-24 in the Slight/Enhanced/Marginal Risk areas) Wednesday afternoon. But, if that front moves further north and east, the severe threat will spread north and east with it. Now is the time to start making plans for Wednesday afternoon and evening. Have multiple ways to get warnings and keep your cell phones on as the severe threat will persist into the evening and possibly into the overnight hours early Thursday morning. Damaging wind gusts remain the primary threat with any severe thunderstorms that develop, but large hail, flooding, and a few tornadoes will all be possible. Stay tuned for updates and any changes to the forecast for Wednesday!

column9: You have may have seen this graphic in many forms today, and you probably have questions about what it means.  This graphic is depicting the likelihood of seeing severe weather in different parts of the area, with the highest likelihood being across the red ("moderate risk") area and the lower likelihood being in the green ("marginal risk").  BUT this doesn't tell you the whole story, and there are some important things you need to be aware of.It has been pointed out that last year's devastating tornadoes that hit Nashville and Cookeville occurred in a green/marginal risk threat area. Why did this happen? Because the conditions that night were "marginal" for tornadoes: We had very strong winds in place, but the atmospheric energy that is needed for strong storms was barely there. 9 times out of 10 this combination of strong winds and low atmospheric energy leads to either weak/brief tornadoes or none at all. Last year's storms were the exception to this rule, and proof that just because a risk is LOW does not mean it is ZERO. So what does this mean for tonight? If you are in the yellow or dark green area, you are once again looking at conditions that are not extremely favorable for strong tornadoes, yet they can't be ruled out. Those conditions get more favorable in the orange ("enhanced") area, and very favorable further south across MS and AL.  However just because you are in a lower risk area, it doesn't mean you are in a zero risk area, and for this reason we want EVERYONE to treat tonight's storm threat seriously. Don't worry about where you are on this map, just be sure you are ready to take action in case we issue a warning for your area.

column9: Wednesday severe storm threat (Tuesday AM Update): The severe threat has increased for the southwest portion of the mid state as of this morning. Unfortunately that means the threat of damaging winds, large hail, flash flooding, and even tornadoes has increased mainly for the southwest, but again, everyone in the mid state needs to remain weather aware for Wednesday. From yesterday's post, we mentioned the position of the warm front will have the greatest impact on the environment Wednesday afternoon and evening, and that remains true. Models want to bring the warm front into the area oriented along I-24 (with the warmest and most unstable air south and west of I-24 in the Slight/Enhanced/Marginal Risk areas) Wednesday afternoon. But, if that front moves further north and east, the severe threat will spread north and east with it. Now is the time to start making plans for Wednesday afternoon and evening. Have multiple ways to get warnings and keep your cell phones on as the severe threat will persist into the evening and possibly into the overnight hours early Thursday morning. Damaging wind gusts remain the primary threat with any severe thunderstorms that develop, but large hail, flooding, and a few tornadoes will all be possible. Stay tuned for updates and any changes to the forecast for Wednesday!

column9: You have may have seen this graphic in many forms today, and you probably have questions about what it means.  This graphic is depicting the likelihood of seeing severe weather in different parts of the area, with the highest likelihood being across the red ("moderate risk") area and the lower likelihood being in the green ("marginal risk").  BUT this doesn't tell you the whole story, and there are some important things you need to be aware of.It has been pointed out that last year's devastating tornadoes that hit Nashville and Cookeville occurred in a green/marginal risk threat area. Why did this happen? Because the conditions that night were "marginal" for tornadoes: We had very strong winds in place, but the atmospheric energy that is needed for strong storms was barely there. 9 times out of 10 this combination of strong winds and low atmospheric energy leads to either weak/brief tornadoes or none at all. Last year's storms were the exception to this rule, and proof that just because a risk is LOW does not mean it is ZERO. So what does this mean for tonight? If you are in the yellow or dark green area, you are once again looking at conditions that are not extremely favorable for strong tornadoes, yet they can't be ruled out. Those conditions get more favorable in the orange ("enhanced") area, and very favorable further south across MS and AL.  However just because you are in a lower risk area, it doesn't mean you are in a zero risk area, and for this reason we want EVERYONE to treat tonight's storm threat seriously. Don't worry about where you are on this map, just be sure you are ready to take action in case we issue a warning for your area.

column9: Wednesday severe storm threat (Tuesday AM Update): The severe threat has increased for the southwest portion of the mid state as of this morning. Unfortunately that means the threat of damaging winds, large hail, flash flooding, and even tornadoes has increased mainly for the southwest, but again, everyone in the mid state needs to remain weather aware for Wednesday. From yesterday's post, we mentioned the position of the warm front will have the greatest impact on the environment Wednesday afternoon and evening, and that remains true. Models want to bring the warm front into the area oriented along I-24 (with the warmest and most unstable air south and west of I-24 in the Slight/Enhanced/Marginal Risk areas) Wednesday afternoon. But, if that front moves further north and east, the severe threat will spread north and east with it. Now is the time to start making plans for Wednesday afternoon and evening. Have multiple ways to get warnings and keep your cell phones on as the severe threat will persist into the evening and possibly into the overnight hours early Thursday morning. Damaging wind gusts remain the primary threat with any severe thunderstorms that develop, but large hail, flooding, and a few tornadoes will all be possible. Stay tuned for updates and any changes to the forecast for Wednesday!

Today (Monday) is a day that you need to pay VERY close attention to the weather if you are in Oklahoma or north Texas, especially in western Oklahoma and adjacent parts of Texas.
We expect storms to begin this morning as potential hail producers. While these storms may produce severe hail (1 inch diameter or more), they will most likely be only marginally severe at worst.
Around noon, the scenario changes. Storms are expected to take on supercell structures, and such storms can produce very large hail, very damaging winds, and tornadoes. This risk will begin initially across western Oklahoma and Texas, then expand quickly east through the afternoon, and continue well into the evening.
By late evening and overnight, storms are expected to merge into a large area, and will mainly pose a risk of flooding (possibly serious flooding) and strong winds. Hail and tornadoes will still be possible, but not as likely as in the afternoon and evening.
The storms are expected to clear from west to east overnight, finally becoming non-severe or east of our forecast area sometime Tuesday morning.
Additional severe weather will be possible again Wednesday and Thursday, but the extent and magnitude of the storms those days are expected to be less than today's.
Have a plan, and use it if severe weather threatens your location.

Today (Monday) is a day that you need to pay VERY close attention to the weather if you are in Oklahoma or north Texas, especially in western Oklahoma and adjacent parts of Texas.
We expect storms to begin this morning as potential hail producers. While these storms may produce severe hail (1 inch diameter or more), they will most likely be only marginally severe at worst.
Around noon, the scenario changes. Storms are expected to take on supercell structures, and such storms can produce very large hail, very damaging winds, and tornadoes. This risk will begin initially across western Oklahoma and Texas, then expand quickly east through the afternoon, and continue well into the evening.
By late evening and overnight, storms are expected to merge into a large area, and will mainly pose a risk of flooding (possibly serious flooding) and strong winds. Hail and tornadoes will still be possible, but not as likely as in the afternoon and evening.
The storms are expected to clear from west to east overnight, finally becoming non-severe or east of our forecast area sometime Tuesday morning.
Additional severe weather will be possible again Wednesday and Thursday, but the extent and magnitude of the storms those days are expected to be less than today's.
Have a plan, and use it if severe weather threatens your location.
